chapter_theme: The battle after the vina contest: Civakan's companions, born on his birthday, fight the suitor kings with a warrior's courtesy (sparing a crippled chariot, resting a foe's horse) while Devadattan, Nabulan, Vipulan and Puttisenan cut through the host; then Nandattan speaks the mantra into the horses' ears, the chariot rises and wheels beyond sight, and Civakan's arrows strip and kill the kings, sparing the good-minded, while ghouls make a feast and a dance of the field.

cast.role: the hero, son of Saccandan and Vijayai, called சீவகசாமி in the invocation
one of Civakan's companions, a horseman
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Vipulan
one of Civakan's companions, brother of Nabulan
one of Civakan's companions, an archer
kings who came seeking the princess
the army of the kings ranged against Civakan after the vina contest

781.reading: Civakan's companions, as if their fierce weapons were hungry and must be fed, cut down elephants, hack horses, smash running chariots and strike so that the warriors' lives may go and enter heaven.
781.event: Civakan's companions cut down the elephants, horses, chariots and warriors of the rival kings.

claims.claim: a warrior slain in battle goes to heaven

781.nuance: The killing is framed as a gift to the slain: the blow is dealt so that the foe's life may enter துறக்கம், the warrior's heaven, a belief the verse gives to the fighters rather than to a school.

782.reading: They call on all who can to come and prove their manhood against them, loose their iron only at the chest of a man who meets them, and offer their own chests, ploughed by fierce elephants' tusks, to lie scarred and beautiful.
782.event: The companions challenge the enemy and strike only at foes who face them.

claims.claim: a chest scarred by an elephant's tusk is a warrior's beauty

782.nuance: Line 2 states a rule of fair fight: no weapon is thrown except at the chest of one who has accepted the combat (ஏற்றவர்), so a fleeing man is spared.

783.reading: Brandishing their swords, eyes blazing red, they turn back charging elephants with the spear, cut an enemy chariot's ropes with the sword and drive off its horses, and then tell the charioteer to bring faultless ones and yoke them.
783.event: The companions disable an enemy chariot and bid its charioteer re-yoke it with fresh horses.
783.nuance: The courtesy is the point: having crippled the chariot they do not strike the helpless man in it but bid him re-equip and fight on; பாகந் யென்று in line 4 looks like a misdivided பாக நீ என்று.

784.reading: They tell a foe to rest his tired horse a little from the fight, meet the king with their burning spears, and laugh that the lady's wedding is a fine thing for them; like lions and tigers were Civakan's companions.
784.event: The companions spare a foe's weary horse, face the enemy king and laugh in battle.
784.nuance: The laughter of line 3 makes the wedding a jest: the battle is the companions' share of Civakan's marriage feast.

785.reading: Born on the very day Civakan was born, with drum-like shoulders as if plaited with iron, lovers of the elephant-and-spear fight, they call out that a hundred of them stand ready for a hundred crore: such were they.
785.event: The companions challenge the enemy host, a hundred against a hundred crore.
785.nuance: That the companions were born on Civakan's birthday ties their valour to his destiny; the number நூற்றுவர் may be the companions' band or a boast, the verse does not say which.

786.reading: Like a potter's wheel spun hard, the bridled horse of Devadattan, mighty with the sword, splits the throng of spears, sinks the elephants' foreheads into pools of blood and wheels about scattering the kings' crests, garlands and crown-jewels.
786.event: Devadattan's horse wheels through the enemy, scattering the kings' crowns and jewels.
786.nuance: Line 3's இருங்குளம் பழுத்தி is hard; the sense of the elephants' foreheads sunk in pools is a guess.

787.reading: Foes wonder whether a bridled horse leapt or a bird; the kings' bellies burn as they cry 'Nabula! Vipula!', and the two, angered, wear down the elephants' face-plates with their horses' hooves and take the tilaka from the kings' crowned heads.
787.event: Nabulan and Vipulan ride down the enemy elephants and strip the kings of their crown ornaments.

788.reading: As the curved pods of the thorny silk-cotton tree, smeared as with red paste, ripen on every branch under the cloud, so the fresh heads of the garlanded warriors fall to the arrows of the red-eyed one who bears the name of Tiru.
788.event: A companion named after Tiru shoots down the enemy warriors' heads.
788.nuance: திருவின் பேரான் (one who bears Tiru's name) is not resolved in the verse: it could point to a companion whose name holds Sri or the lotus; மாயங்கொல் in line 3 (is it magic?) frames the falling heads as a wonder.

789.reading: Like a dark cloud that has drunk the blue sea and stands heavy in the sky, Puttisenan, master of hidden lore, scatters gold-decked arrows and makes the spear-bright army of the kings a feast for Death.
789.event: Puttisenan rains arrows on the kings' army.
789.nuance: கூற்றிற்கு லிருந்து in line 4 reads as கூற்றிற்கு விருந்து, a feast for Death, the same hospitality figure Civakan turns on the kings in 798.

790.reading: Warriors stand with heroic spears all round their bodies and red blood streaming, looking like chariot-wheel hubs set with spokes and capped with a jewelled band.

791.reading: The poet turns: so here the kings who wanted the golden lady's embrace and the young men are locked in confused sword-war; now he will tell of the spear-bearer over there.
791.event: The narrator leaves the companions' fight to turn to Civakan.

792.reading: Civakan looks at his younger brother and asks him, skilled both in the chowrie-crowned horses' ears and in the heroic mantra, to speak it to end their danger.
792.event: Civakan bids Nandattan recite the war mantra into the horses' ears.
792.nuance: Nandattan is his charioteer here; the mantra is a battle craft he has, not a rite of worship.

793.reading: Hearing the mantra, the four horses climb as if to leap into the sky, the wheels leave the ground, and the two, held in women's eyes, take guard of a sky-field that neither men nor iron can reach.
793.event: Under the mantra the chariot rises into the air.
793.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are knotted; the reading that the women hold the two heroes in their eyes and that the sky is beyond men and weapons is a guess.

794.reading: Testing the reins and holding the goad in his right hand, he pricks the horse, saying 'let victory be won'; the poet says he cannot tell it, but the bell-ringing golden chariot seized the ears and eyes of the army.
794.event: Nandattan urges the horses on and the army is held by the sight and sound of the chariot.
794.nuance: மொழிதல் தேற்றேன் (I cannot say) is the poet's own aside inside the action.

795.reading: Men say the lord's chariot is a bird, formless, then with form, on earth, then in the sky, in the mind, then in the face, in the eye, then in the ear, while he, gazing past the rules of the treatise, takes the prescribed track and drives his circles.
795.event: The enemy cannot follow the chariot as it wheels in circles.
795.nuance: அருவம் and உருவம் are the vocabulary of doctrine (the formless and the formed) used for a chariot too swift to place; நூல் கழிய can mean beyond the bounds of the chariot manual.

796.reading: Its wheel a whirled firebrand of aloe-wood that grazes on dear lives, its speed shaming lightning in the clouds, showing wings that swallow all rivalry, the young hero's golden chariot flies like the chariot that carries the day.

797.reading: Diamond garlands with cut strings, white umbrellas overturned, peacock plumes fallen, armour stripped, chowries cut and bowstrings snapped: the deluded kings' hearts fail, and as the generous one's arrow pressed, their bows bent and gave up.
797.event: Civakan's archery strips the kings of umbrellas, armour and bowstrings and breaks their will.
797.nuance: Line 4 is compressed: whether the bow that bends and stops is Civakan's or the kings' is not certain; the overturned white umbrellas are the kings' lost sovereignty.

798.reading: 'You whom the anklet-footed lady beat at the vina, see her hot wide eyes and welcome your guests!', he says, and offers each king a red arrow or two and feeds them as is fitting.
798.event: Civakan taunts the suitor kings and shoots them, one or two arrows each.
798.nuance: The taunt is built on hospitality: the kings came as guests to the contest and are now served arrows, உள்ளவாறு ஊட்டினான், fed as their share deserves.

799.reading: The burning arrows only lick the jewelled chests of good-minded kings, but tear the gold armour of mean-minded ones and take their lives, spreading as if to tell them not to go near evil even in the body they will take next.
799.event: Civakan's arrows graze the good kings and kill the wicked.

claims.claim: one who dies in evil should shun evil in the body of the next birth

799.nuance: The arrows judge: the slaughter is sorted by the kings' minds (நன்மனம், புன்மனம்), so the war of desire becomes a moral sentence that reaches into the next birth.

800.reading: Bowstrings snapped like fish-lines, the stout girths of hill-like elephants cut through, strong chariots overturned with ropes severed, the kings raise their flesh-smeared discuses and roar.
800.event: Their gear cut to pieces, the kings take up their discuses and roar a counter-challenge.

801.reading: Like a jewelled hill against which the roaring rain pours, those who faced the fight roared too; at their roar his strung bow poured arrows like a monsoon cloud, and on this side the flood of blood swept along as he heaped a hill of flesh.
801.event: Civakan answers the kings' roar with a storm of arrows and a flood of blood.

802.reading: Parting with his sharp steel the rain of weapons the angry kings let fly, bending his bow to pour arrows, his shining sword glaring to swallow lives, he swims through the army at play.
802.event: Civakan beats off the kings' weapons and cuts through their army.
802.nuance: விளையாடுகின்றான் (he plays) makes the slaughter a game, the tone the next two verses carry into the ghouls' dance.

803.reading: Using an elephant's white tusk as a toothstick, scraping her tongue with a bloody sword, gargling blood, wearing a garland of dead horses' entrails, dressed in fat for cloth and adorned with white bones, the pregnant she-ghoul dances, and he watches and laughs with delight.
803.event: A pregnant ghoul makes her toilette from the battlefield's remains and dances; Civakan watches and laughs.
803.nuance: The ghoul's acts follow a morning toilette in order (toothstick, tongue-scraping, gargle, garland, cloth, ornaments), so the battlefield becomes her dressing-room.

804.reading: As if to say 'this is the state of the blood-flood from the pale bodies', ghouls with teeth like elephants' nails join hands above their heads and sing and dance over what has been given them; little jackals laugh, elephants trumpet, and eagles and vultures lie with their sides split.
804.event: Ghouls sing and dance over the field while jackals, eagles and vultures gorge.
804.nuance: அளித்தவை பாடி (singing what was given) casts the ghouls as bards praising a patron's gift; விலாவிற்று in line 4 may mean the birds lie gorged till their sides burst or that the elephants lie with ribs broken.

links.note: In 640 some suitors vowed to plunge into battle only if a man other than the vina's victor took her; in 791 the kings who desired her fight after Civakan has won at the vina.
links.teaches: The kings' war breaks the very terms they set at the contest, so their fight is shown as desire that will not accept its own rule, not as a defence of the bride.

links.note: 708 records a king who came and fell in the sea of the vina; 798 has Civakan remind the kings that she beat them at the vina before he serves them arrows.
links.teaches: Civakan's taunt makes the musical defeat the first round of the battle, so the kings now lose twice to the same bride, once to her skill and once to his.

links.note: The patikam's 28 says that his brother, companions and wives renounced and the master of the vina went to the unequalled state; here the same hero laughs with delight at a ghoul dressing in the slain.
links.teaches: The Jain epic lets its hero relish slaughter fully before it turns him to renunciation, so the release it promises in 28 is a turning from a violence he once enjoyed, not from one he never knew.

links.note: Kural 773 calls help to a foe in trouble the cutting edge of valour; 783 has the companions cripple a chariot and then bid its charioteer yoke fresh horses.
links.teaches: The epic turns the couplet's ஊராண்மை into a battlefield move: the generosity is not mercy that ends the fight but an invitation to go on fighting on equal terms.

gains.a: a concept that makes the companions' strange order a recognised height of valour rather than a jest
gains.b: a concrete act that shows what the help to a stricken foe looks like in a chariot fight

links.note: Kural 776 counts as wasted the days without a noble wound; 782 has the companions offer their chests to the tusk so the scar may lie beautiful.
links.teaches: Where the couplet keeps a sober ledger of wounded days, the epic turns the wound into ornament, so the same ethic moves from a reckoning of duty to an aesthetic of the body.

gains.a: the reason a scarred chest should count as beauty: a wound is the record of a day not wasted
gains.b: the place of the noble wound on the body, the chest that faces the foe, which the couplet does not name

links.note: Kural 202 says evil is to be feared more than fire because evil yields evil; in 799 burning arrows kill the mean-minded kings and warn them off evil even in their next body.
links.teaches: The epic makes the fire itself the preacher: the burning arrow that kills is only the lesser fire, and its warning points to the evil that will follow the dead into the next birth.

gains.a: the ground of the arrows' warning, that evil breeds evil and so outlasts the body the fire destroys
gains.b: a picture of evil outlasting death, which gives the couplet's comparison with fire a span beyond one life

links.note: Tirumanthiram 2133 has the subtle body, its old deeds following, take up a new body; 799's arrows warn the slain against evil in the body they will take next.
links.teaches: Held together, the epic's warning to the dying presupposes the passage Tirumular describes, and Tirumular's mechanism is given a moral use: deeds follow, so the dead are urged to change their conduct across the change of body.

gains.a: the mechanism, deeds carried by the subtle body into a new birth, that makes 'the body you will take' literal
gains.b: an ethical address to the dying that the doctrinal account of transmigration leaves out

links.note: Naladiyar 3 has kings who rode under the umbrella fall when their deeds give out; 797 shows the kings' white umbrellas overturned by Civakan's arrows.
links.teaches: The quatrain names only spent deeds as the cause of a king's fall, while the epic shows the immediate cause, an archer and the kings' own desire, and in 799 sorts the fallen by their minds, so karma and the battle are both given as cause.

gains.a: a frame in which the overturned umbrellas are a lesson in impermanence and not only a victory
gains.b: a scene that names the human cause beside the karmic one, which the quatrain's 'other deeds' leaves blank

links.note: Purananuru 369 sings the battlefield as a harvest where the ghoul-woman holds the corpses and jackals thresh, and the bard asks the king for a gift; in 804 ghouls already fed sing over what was given them.
links.teaches: The epic hands the bard's role to the ghouls: in the Puram poem the singer asks for a share of the field, while here the scavengers have had their share and their song is thanks, so the field is a patron's gift completed.

gains.a: the kalavazhi frame that explains why ghouls 'sing what was given', as bards sing a patron's bounty
gains.b: the reversal that shows how close the Puram bard stands to the scavengers who share the same harvest of corpses

links.note: Maduraikkanchi 24-42 sets fat-mouthed demon women dancing the tunangai around a battle-sacrifice whose cook serves flesh-rice to the soldiers; in 803 a pregnant ghoul dresses herself in the field's remains while Civakan watches and laughs.
links.teaches: The Sangam poem makes the ghouls' feast part of a rite the king performs, while the epic removes the rite and keeps the dance as a spectacle for the hero's delight, so the motif survives as ornament of heroism.

gains.a: the ritual setting from which the battlefield ghoul descends, which makes Civakan's laughter a presiding king's pleasure
gains.b: a later afterlife of its demon women, cut loose from sacrifice and turned into a toilette parody

source_issues: Verses 781, 783, 787, 790, 794, 795 and 800 carry repaired TSCII slips (ோ் read as ேர்); the repaired readings make sense.
Verses 796 and 798 were printed in eight half-lines and have been joined into four.
Verse 783 line 4 prints பாகந் யென்று, apparently a misdivided பாக நீ என்று.
Verse 789 line 4 prints கூற்றிற்கு லிருந்து, apparently for கூற்றிற்கு விருந்து.
Verse 798 line 1 prints வடியி னாடன், apparently for அடியினாள் தன் (the anklet-footed lady's).
